To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

social safety nets can play a key role in reducing the poverty of persons with disabilities, and that the design of safety nets can be improved by incorporating the perspectives of people with disabilities in all stages of the design process.
disability is often associated with poverty, and that social safety nets may play a role in reducing this poverty.

disability is an important factor in determining the poverty status of households, and that disability-targeting and mainstreaming are complementary ways of addressing the needs of persons with disabilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How do safety nets reach persons with disabilities in developing and transition countries?
how social safety net programs can be designed and implemented so that they are inclusive of persons with disabilities in developing and transition countries.
how to make social protection systems more responsive to the needs of persons with disabilities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
disability mainstreaming is the most appropriate strategy for reaching persons with disabilities in social safety nets, but that disability targeting can also be an effective approach.
there is a clear need for more research and evaluation on the inclusion of disability considerations in social safety nets in developing countries.
the evidence base on disability and social protection is weak, but there is a strong case for including disability in social safety net programs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social safety net programs should be disability inclusive, and disability specific programs should be mainstreamed.
disability inclusion in social safety net programs should be a priority in all countries.

disability mainstreaming should be the first choice for social safety nets in developing countries, but disability targeting should also be considered, and may be the only feasible option in some situations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inclusion of disability considerations in safety nets is not only possible, but also desirable.
the design of safety nets should be based on a clear analysis of the needs of persons with disabilities in the context of the social and economic conditions in which they live.
disability mainstreaming is the preferred option.
